anatomy.intro: Narrow fleshy leaves cluster around the tips of spreading, branching stems.

parts.function: A narrow, pointed succulent leaf carries stored water.
parts.label: Fleshy leaf

parts.function: Leaves cluster around the end of an extending shoot.
parts.label: Shoot tip

parts.function: The reddish stem supports leaves beyond the original crown.
parts.label: Branching stem

parts.function: A node marks a leaf's attachment along the stem.
parts.label: Leaf node

flowers.text: White, lightly scented stars gather in fairly flat clusters. Look closely at a flower’s center for the stamens, the slender pollen-bearing parts surrounding the center.

growth.note: Follow new shoots and branching over time; leaf color can shift with growing conditions.

stages.text: Short shoots hold the copper-toned foliage close together.
stages.title: Small leafy shoot

stages.text: Stems extend and turn upward at their tips.
stages.title: Spreading branches

stages.text: Established growth may produce pale flower clusters.
stages.title: Mature flowering shoot

habitat.text: Sedum adolphi comes from Mexico and grows as a low succulent subshrub. Its stems spread along the ground before turning upward at their tips, allowing the plant to extend sideways while keeping its leafy shoots raised.

lookalikes.name: Pale rosette echeveria
lookalikes.text: Compare its broad powdery leaves and compact crown with the sedum's narrower leaves on visible stems.

mature.text: NParks lists roughly 20 cm height and 60–90 cm spread for S. adolphi. That broad, low habit explains how its stems can gradually weave through neighboring rosettes in a container.

milestones.text: Acquired in the Smart Planet Home mixed succulent garden from Home Depot.
milestones.title: Joined the collection

milestones.text: The rosettes, copper-toned shoots and broad paddles stayed together in the terra-cotta planter.
milestones.title: Repotted together

nameStory.text: Coppertone describes the warm tint of the leaves. NParks lists Sedum nussbaumerianum as a synonym of S. adolphi, explaining why both names occur in horticulture.
